newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's central bank cuts rates.
newsitem.headline: Australia's central bank cuts rates.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia on Wednesday cut official interest rates for the fifth time in a year, trimming 0.5 percentage points off cash rates to 5.0 percent, citing low inflation and room for faster growth.

"This change, like the four previous reductions in interest rates over the past year, is based on the improving picture for Australia's medium-term inflation performance, which opens up scope for faster growth and employment," the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said.
Economists welcomed the rate cut, which they said was expected, but added that the timing had surprised the market because a reduction had been tipped for next week.
"The only oddity in the whole thing was the timing," said Michael Blythe, senior economist of the Commonwealth Bank.

"Just about everybody has been expecting a rate cut in the very short term, and the RBA has come through. Certainly, with inflation dead in the water and unemployment still high, there seems to be no reason not to cut rates," Blythe said.
In fact, some economists said the bank's bullish reasoning for its fifth rate cut may even suggest it believes there is room for a further reduction in interest rates.
"There might be some attempt to price in another rate cut," said Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust.
Tony Meer, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the bank's comment that the economy had room to grow in the next two to three years without threatening inflation was significant.
"It suggests the bank sees enough room for yet another easing, if not two," Meer said.
Official cash rates were 7.5 percent a year ago.

In a two-page statement announcing the cut, the bank said that in the year to June, the underlying rate of inflation was 1.7 percent and that it expected underlying inflation to stay below two percent into 1998.
It also said that economic growth in 1997 had been picking up, but that it remained moderate. Economic growth was an annual 2.4 percent in the March quarter.
"The crucial test for monetary policy is to have the setting that will best contribute to low inflation and economic growth in the long run," the bank said.

"Monetary policy cannot fine-tune the cycle or manufacture sustained high rates of real growth...however, monetary policy should not stand in the way of a period of stronger growth that can be accommodated without breaching the inflation objective."
The bank said that although earlier rate cuts were still "working their way through the economy", it believed the latest reduction would not fuel inflation.
"The balance of risks at this time is such as to favour this further easing of monetary policy," the bank said.
